reference.source: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics / relevant specialty textbook
clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant vascular dysplasia most often caused by variants in ENG or ACVRL1, with SMAD4 variants producing a combined HHT and juvenile polyposis phenotype
Recurrent spontaneous epistaxis is usually the earliest and most frequent manifestation, often from childhood
Mucocutaneous telangiectases characteristically appear on the lips, tongue, face and fingertips
Visceral arteriovenous malformations occur in the lungs, liver and brain and can cause serious complications well before overt symptoms
Pulmonary arteriovenous malformations create a right-to-left shunt with risk of paradoxical embolic stroke and cerebral abscess, so contrast echocardiography screening is important
The Curacao clinical criteria (epistaxis, telangiectases, visceral involvement, affected first-degree relative) support diagnosis, confirmed by genetic testing
The causative genes encode components of the TGF-beta/BMP signalling pathway that maintains normal vascular integrity
reference.pathophysiology: Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia is an autosomal dominant disorder of vascular development caused by loss-of-function variants in genes of the transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-beta)/bone morphogenetic protein signalling pathway, principally ENG (endoglin) and ACVRL1 (ALK1), with SMAD4 accounting for the combined syndrome with juvenile polyposis. Disruption of this pathway impairs the normal balance of signals controlling endothelial proliferation, vessel maturation and mural cell recruitment. The result is fragile, dilated telangiectatic vessels and larger arteriovenous malformations lacking an intervening capillary bed, which bleed readily and, in the case of pulmonary lesions, permit right-to-left shunting.
additionalDifferentials: Isolated recurrent epistaxis from local nasal causes
Von Willebrand disease and other bleeding disorders
Cutaneous or hepatic vascular malformations of other cause
additionalInvestigations: Germline molecular genetic testing of ENG, ACVRL1 and SMAD4
Transthoracic contrast (bubble) echocardiography to screen for pulmonary arteriovenous malformations
CT of the chest to characterise pulmonary arteriovenous malformations when screening is positive
Contrast-enhanced brain MRI for cerebral vascular malformations per guidelines
Liver imaging (Doppler ultrasound or cross-sectional) for hepatic arteriovenous malformations
Full blood count and iron studies to assess bleeding-related anaemia; colonoscopy if SMAD4-related
redFlags: Neurological deficit from paradoxical embolic stroke or cerebral abscess via a pulmonary shunt
Massive epistaxis or gastrointestinal bleeding causing haemodynamic compromise
High-output cardiac failure from extensive hepatic arteriovenous malformations
Haemoptysis or spontaneous haemothorax from a pulmonary arteriovenous malformation, especially in pregnancy
reference.prognosis: With screening and treatment of visceral arteriovenous malformations, many life-threatening complications are preventable, and most affected individuals have a near-normal life expectancy. Chronic epistaxis and gastrointestinal bleeding, however, cause substantial iron-deficiency anaemia and reduced quality of life over time.
pitfalls: Managing recurrent epistaxis without screening for occult pulmonary or cerebral arteriovenous malformations
Omitting antibiotic prophylaxis for procedures in patients with pulmonary arteriovenous malformations at risk of abscess
Missing the SMAD4-associated juvenile polyposis phenotype and its cancer surveillance needs
Under-recognising the condition in relatives because features and severity vary within families
references: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
